questions.question: What is a stack and what are its core operations?
questions.title: Stack Data Structure Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **stack** is a LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) data structure. The last element pushed is the first element popped. Core operations: `push` (add to top), `pop` (remove from top), `peek` (view top without removing) — all O(1).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of LIFO principle and common use cases like recursion call stack, undo operations, balanced parentheses
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using the legacy Stack class in Java instead of ArrayDeque, or not knowing real-world applications
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that in Java you should use ArrayDeque as a stack (not the legacy Stack class) and name 2-3 concrete applications

sections.title: LIFO — Last In, First Out
sections.content: Think of a stack of plates — you add to the top and take from the top. In Java, **use `ArrayDeque<Integer>` as a stack** (not the legacy `Stack` class which is synchronized and slower). Methods: `push()` / `addFirst()`, `pop()` / `removeFirst()`, `peek()` / `peekFirst()`. All O(1). Common applications: **function call stack**, undo/redo, balanced parentheses validation, expression evaluation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- LIFO: Last-In, First-Out
- push: add to top — O(1)
- pop: remove from top — O(1)
- peek: view top without removal — O(1)
- Java: prefer `ArrayDeque` over legacy `Stack` class
- Real use cases: JVM call stack, browser back button, undo operations
- Balanced parentheses: push open brackets, pop and match on close brackets

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A stack is a LIFO data structure — last in, first out. It's like a stack of plates where you always add and remove from the top. The three core operations are push to add to the top, pop to remove from the top, and peek to look at the top without removing — all O(1). In Java I'd use ArrayDeque rather than the legacy Stack class because it's faster and not synchronized. Real-world uses include the JVM call stack, undo operations in editors, and the classic balanced parentheses problem.

questions.question: What is a queue and how does it differ from a stack?
questions.title: Queue Data Structure Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **queue** is a FIFO (First-In-First-Out) data structure — the first element added is the first removed. Core operations: `enqueue` (add to rear), `dequeue` (remove from front), `peek` (view front) — all O(1). Use `ArrayDeque` or `LinkedList` in Java.

interviewer_intent.testing: FIFO understanding and practical Java usage — BFS uses a queue, task scheduling uses a queue
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing which end elements enter and leave, or not knowing the Java Queue interface
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect queue to BFS traversal and mention PriorityQueue for when ordering matters

sections.title: FIFO — First In, First Out
sections.content: A queue is like a line of people — first person to join is first to be served. Elements enter at the **rear (offer/add)** and leave from the **front (poll/remove)**. In Java, `Queue<Integer> q = new LinkedList<>()` or `new ArrayDeque<>()`. Key methods: `offer()` (add to rear), `poll()` (remove from front, returns null if empty), `peek()` (view front without removing). Essential for **BFS traversal** of trees and graphs.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- FIFO: First-In, First-Out — opposite of stack
- offer/add: enqueue at rear — O(1)
- poll/remove: dequeue from front — O(1)
- peek: view front without removal — O(1)
- Java: ArrayDeque (preferred) or LinkedList implements Queue
- PriorityQueue: elements dequeued by priority not insertion order
- Real use: BFS, task scheduling, message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A queue is the opposite of a stack — it's FIFO, first in first out, like a line at a bank. Elements are added at the rear and removed from the front. In Java I'd declare it as Queue with an ArrayDeque implementation. The main methods are offer to add, poll to remove from the front, and peek to view the front. The most important application I'd mention is BFS — breadth-first search — which uses a queue to process nodes level by level. If I need ordering by priority instead of insertion order, I'd use a PriorityQueue.

questions.question: How do you check for balanced parentheses using a stack?
questions.title: Balanced Parentheses Stack Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Push opening brackets onto the stack.** When a closing bracket is encountered, pop from the stack and check if it matches. If the stack is empty at the end, brackets are balanced. O(n) time, O(n) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Classic stack application — tests whether you can map a problem to the right data structure
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to check if the stack is empty before popping (NullPointerException on empty stack), or not handling the case where stack is non-empty at the end
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Handle all three bracket types — (), [], {} — and walk through both a valid and invalid example

sections.title: Stack-Based Bracket Matching
sections.content: Iterate through each character. If it's an **opening bracket** `(`, `[`, `{` — push it. If it's a **closing bracket**: first check if stack is empty (if so, unbalanced — return false). Pop from stack and verify it matches the corresponding opening bracket. After the full scan, return `stack.isEmpty()` — any leftover unmatched opening brackets means unbalanced.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Push opening brackets: (, [, {
- On closing bracket: check stack not empty, pop, verify match
- Use a Map: ')' → '(', ']' → '[', '}' → '{' for clean matching
- Final check: stack must be empty
- Time: O(n), Space: O(n) worst case (all opening brackets)
- Edge cases: empty string (return true), starts with closing bracket (return false)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I iterate through each character. If I see an opening bracket, I push it onto the stack. If I see a closing bracket, I first check if the stack is empty — if it is, there's no matching opener so I return false. Otherwise I pop from the stack and check if it's the corresponding opener. At the end, the stack must be empty — any remaining openers are unmatched. I'd use a HashMap mapping each closing bracket to its expected opening bracket to keep the matching logic clean. Edge cases to mention: empty stack before pop, and non-empty stack after scanning all characters.

questions.question: What is ArrayDeque and why is it preferred over Stack and LinkedList for stack/queue operations in Java?
questions.title: ArrayDeque vs Stack vs LinkedList Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **ArrayDeque** is a resizable array implementation of a double-ended queue. It is preferred because it has **no synchronization overhead** (unlike the legacy Stack), **better cache performance** than LinkedList (contiguous memory), and supports both stack and queue operations efficiently.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the idiomatic modern Java collections and can justify your choice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Stack (legacy, synchronized, slower) or LinkedList (node overhead, cache unfriendly) when ArrayDeque is better
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Stack extends Vector which is synchronized — that's why it's avoided in single-threaded code

sections.title: Why ArrayDeque Wins
sections.content: Java's legacy `Stack` class **extends Vector**, which is synchronized — every push/pop acquires a lock even in single-threaded code, causing unnecessary overhead. `LinkedList` uses node objects with `prev`/`next` pointers — lots of object creation and cache-unfriendly memory layout. `ArrayDeque` uses a **circular array** — fast, cache-friendly, no synchronization, and resizes automatically. It implements both `Deque` (as a stack) and `Queue` interfaces.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Stack (legacy): extends Vector, synchronized, avoid it
- LinkedList: O(1) but pointer overhead and cache misses
- ArrayDeque: circular array, cache-friendly, no sync overhead
- As stack: push=addFirst, pop=removeFirst, peek=peekFirst
- As queue: offer=addLast, poll=removeFirst, peek=peekFirst
- Java docs explicitly recommend ArrayDeque over Stack
- Not thread-safe — use Deque from java.util.concurrent if needed

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I always use ArrayDeque for stack and queue operations. The legacy Stack class extends Vector which is synchronized, so every operation acquires a lock — that's unnecessary overhead in single-threaded code. LinkedList works but creates node objects with pointer overhead and is cache-unfriendly since nodes are scattered in memory. ArrayDeque uses a circular array which is cache-friendly and resizes automatically. The Java documentation itself recommends ArrayDeque over Stack. For both stack operations like push and pop and queue operations like offer and poll, ArrayDeque handles both.

questions.question: What are the real-world use cases of Stack and Queue in software engineering?
questions.title: Stack and Queue Real-World Use Cases
questions.direct_answer: **Stack** use cases: function call stack (JVM manages method frames), undo/redo in editors, balanced bracket checking, DFS graph traversal. **Queue** use cases: BFS graph traversal, task schedulers, print spoolers, message queues (Kafka/RabbitMQ), and producer-consumer pipelines.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can connect data structure theory to software you've used or built — shows practical awareness.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving only textbook examples (push/pop) without connecting to real systems like Kafka or the JVM call stack.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the JVM call stack is literally a stack — StackOverflowError happens when it exceeds its depth limit due to infinite recursion.

rows: Last function called is first to return
Most recent action is undone first
Explore latest branch fully before backtracking
Most recent opener must close first
Process nodes level by level in order
Tasks processed in order of arrival
Messages consumed in order they were produced

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Stacks appear everywhere LIFO order is natural. The JVM call stack is the most fundamental — every method call pushes a frame, and when the method returns it pops. That's why infinite recursion causes StackOverflowError. Undo in editors is also a stack — most recent action undone first. Queues are ideal when order of arrival matters: BFS uses a queue to process nodes level by level, and message queues like Kafka ensure messages are consumed in the order they were produced.

questions.question: How do you implement a stack using two queues?
questions.title: Stack Using Two Queues Java
questions.direct_answer: Implement push as O(n) by adding to q2, moving all of q1 to q2, then swapping q1 and q2 — or make pop O(n) by moving elements between queues at pop time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of stack/queue semantics and ability to simulate one with the other
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overcomplicating the solution or not choosing which operation to make expensive
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Present both variants (push-heavy vs pop-heavy) and explain the trade-off

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
There are two variants of this problem: make push expensive or make pop expensive. I'll describe the push-heavy variant which is more commonly asked.

You maintain two queues, q1 and q2. For push: add the new element to q2, then dequeue everything from q1 into q2, then swap the names of q1 and q2. Now q1 has the new element at the front and everything else behind it in reverse insertion order — which is exactly LIFO order. Pop and peek just operate on the front of q1.

Let me trace through: push 1, push 2, push 3. After pushing 1: q1=[1]. After pushing 2: add 2 to q2, move 1 from q1 to q2, swap — q1=[2,1]. After pushing 3: add 3 to q2, move 2,1 from q1 to q2, swap — q1=[3,2,1]. Pop returns 3 — correct LIFO order.

The pop-heavy variant is the inverse: push just adds to q1, but pop moves all elements except the last from q1 to q2 and returns the last.

Time complexity: the push-heavy variant has O(n) push and O(1) pop. The pop-heavy variant has O(1) push and O(n) pop. Which to use depends on whether reads or writes are more frequent in your use case.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Push-heavy: on push, add to q2, drain q1 into q2, swap — O(n) push, O(1) pop
Pop-heavy: on pop, drain q1 into q2 except last, return last — O(1) push, O(n) pop
One queue variant also exists: on push, enqueue then rotate by (size-1) dequeue/enqueues
Useful to understand LIFO vs FIFO semantics deeply

questions.question: How do you use a stack to evaluate a mathematical expression?
questions.title: Stack Evaluate Expression Java
questions.direct_answer: For postfix expressions, push operands onto a stack and when you encounter an operator, pop two operands, apply the operator, and push the result back.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical stack application — shows understanding of stack as a computation aid
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing infix and postfix evaluation, or getting the operand order wrong for non-commutative operators
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the operand order: for A B -, you pop B first then A, and compute A minus B

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
There are two parts to expression evaluation: infix (the normal human notation like 3 + 4) and postfix or reverse Polish notation like 3 4 +. Postfix is easier to evaluate with a stack and is often what interview problems use.

For postfix evaluation: scan left to right. If the token is a number, push it onto the stack. If the token is an operator, pop two numbers, apply the operator, and push the result. At the end, the single remaining value on the stack is the answer.

Operand order matters for non-commutative operators. When you pop for subtraction or division, the first pop gives the right operand and the second pop gives the left operand. So for the expression 8 3 -, pop 3 first (right), pop 8 second (left), compute 8 minus 3 equals 5.

For infix evaluation, you need two stacks — one for operators and one for operands — and you apply operator precedence rules when pushing. This is the Shunting Yard algorithm. It's more complex but works on standard mathematical notation.

In Java, you'd use a Deque implemented as an ArrayDeque as the stack. For a simple postfix evaluator with only +, -, *, / on integers, the code is straightforward: split the expression string, iterate the tokens, and switch on each operator.

This pattern is commonly seen in coding problems like LeetCode 150 (Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation).

sections.title: Key Points
content: Postfix evaluation: number → push; operator → pop two, compute, push result
Order: first pop is right operand, second pop is left operand (matters for - and /)
Infix evaluation: two stacks + operator precedence (Shunting Yard algorithm)
Use ArrayDeque as Stack in Java — preferred over the legacy Stack class

questions.question: What is a monotonic stack and what problems does it solve?
questions.title: Monotonic Stack Pattern Java
questions.direct_answer: A monotonic stack maintains elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order by popping elements that violate the order before pushing — used for next greater/smaller element problems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of a common interview pattern beyond basic stack push/pop
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Solving next-greater-element with O(n²) nested loops instead of the O(n) monotonic stack
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the invariant: what the stack contains at any point and why popping an element resolves its answer

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A monotonic stack is a stack where the elements are always in sorted order — either always increasing from bottom to top, or always decreasing. You maintain this invariant by popping elements that would violate the order before pushing a new element.

The classic problem it solves is Next Greater Element: for each element in an array, find the first element to its right that is greater. The brute force is O(n²) nested loops. With a monotonic stack, it's O(n).

Here's how it works for a decreasing stack: iterate left to right. For each element, while the stack is not empty and the top of the stack is smaller than the current element, pop the top — and record that the current element is the 'next greater' for the popped element. Then push the current element. Elements still on the stack when we finish have no greater element to their right.

The key insight is: when we pop an element, we've just found its answer. The element that caused the pop is the next greater element for everything we just popped.

This pattern also applies to: largest rectangle in histogram, daily temperatures, trapping rainwater, and stock span problems. All of them involve 'find the next element that is bigger or smaller' and all benefit from the O(n) monotonic stack approach.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Maintains sorted order by popping violating elements before each push
O(n) solution to next-greater/next-smaller element problems (vs O(n²) brute force)
When you pop an element, the current element is its answer
Applications: histogram areas, daily temperatures, stock span, trapping rainwater
